relationships.description: The driving condition, such as a new regulation or a budget squeeze, is linked to a restriction on the solution space that exists because of it or bears on it, without implying that one causes or refines the other.
relationships.evidence: An architecture decision record or constraint register entry cites the driver (e.g. 'GDPR enforcement') as the context or rationale for the stated restriction (e.g. 'customer data must remain in EU regions').

relationships.description: The driving condition is connected to a benefit that a named stakeholder would gain or lose depending on how the organization responds to it, for example rising order-handling cost linked to the value 'saves customers ten minutes per order'.
relationships.evidence: A business case, value map or strategy document lists the stakeholder value alongside the driver it responds to, or the value statement explicitly references the driver as its context.

relationships.description: The driving condition prompts or shapes an analytical finding about the current state, such as market pressure leading to an identified capability gap or risk.
relationships.evidence: A SWOT, gap analysis, risk register or audit report records the finding and names the driver as the condition that triggered or informed the analysis.

relationships.description: One driving condition intensifies, weakens or gives rise to another, for example accumulating technical debt contributing to rising operating cost.
relationships.evidence: A strategy paper, driver tree or motivation model shows the first driver cited as a cause or contributing factor in the description of the second.

relationships.description: The driving condition motivates stakeholders to set, reprioritize or reshape an intended end state, such as a regulation coming into effect prompting a compliance goal.
relationships.evidence: A goal statement in a strategy document, OKR set or roadmap cites the driver as its rationale or 'why' section.

relationships.description: The driving condition affects which measurable result the organization targets or what threshold and time frame it sets, for example a compliance deadline fixing the date by which an outcome must be reached.
relationships.evidence: An outcome definition, KPI target or OKR key result references the driver when justifying its target value or deadline.

relationships.description: The driving condition leads the organization to adopt or revise a general design rule within a scope, such as vendor lock-in concerns giving rise to a cloud-portability principle.
relationships.evidence: The principle's rationale or implications section in the architecture principles catalog names the driver as the reason the principle exists.

relationships.description: The driving condition gives rise to or shapes a specific verifiable 'shall' statement the solution must meet, for example a data-retention regulation producing a requirement to purge records after seven years.
relationships.evidence: The requirement in the backlog or requirements specification carries a traceability link or rationale field pointing to the driver, such as a cited regulation clause.

notes: The two associated-with links are weak: a driver-to-constraint link is usually causal and would be better expressed as influence, as with goals and requirements. Driver-to-value association is vague and may duplicate paths through goals or outcomes.
